sub: The crisis before the Six-Day War

markers.label: Straits of Tiran
markers.description: Egypt closed the straits to Israeli shipping on 22 May 1967, cutting Israel's Red Sea route.

markers.label: Sharm el-Sheikh
markers.description: Egyptian forces controlled the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba from this area.

markers.label: Sinai buildup
markers.description: Egypt moved large forces into Sinai after demanding UNEF's withdrawal.

markers.label: Eilat
markers.description: Israel's Red Sea port was directly affected by the blockade.

slides.title: From Suez Crisis to Six-Day War
slides.cap: Israeli soldiers during the tense 1967 waiting period
slides.body:
The Suez Crisis left a temporary arrangement rather than a peace. UNEF peacekeepers stood in Sinai, the Straits of Tiran remained central to Israel's sea access, and Arab-Israeli rivalry continued through raids, mobilization, and alliance politics.

In May 1967 Egypt ordered UNEF out of Sinai, moved major forces into the peninsula, and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Israel had warned since 1957 that closing the straits would be treated as a casus belli. With reserves mobilized, the economy strained, and Arab armies coordinating around Israel, the waiting period became a national emergency.

stats.lbl: Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran
Israel faced Egypt, Jordan, Syria, and Iraqi support
The blockade, Egyptian deployment in Sinai, and removal of UNEF made the crisis feel like a direct threat to Israel's survival and freedom of navigation.

slides.title: A Small State Surrounded
slides.cap: Israeli soldiers during the tense 1967 waiting period
slides.body:
Israel tried diplomacy while mobilizing reserves. The problem was time: keeping much of the country in uniform could not be sustained for long, and waiting risked allowing enemy deployments to harden. The country was geographically narrow, with its coastal plain only a short distance from the Jordanian-held West Bank and its southern sea route blocked at Tiran.

That is why the victory became so astonishing. Israel began the war under deep pressure, with hostile armies on several fronts, yet within six days it destroyed enemy air forces, broke Egypt's Sinai defenses, captured East Jerusalem and the West Bank from Jordan, and took the Golan Heights from Syria.

stats.lbl: Approximate narrowest width of pre-1967 Israel
Mobilization strained daily life and the economy
Time from opening strike to ceasefire
Israel converted a multi-front strategic crisis into air superiority, rapid maneuver, and territorial victory before its enemies could coordinate a sustained campaign.

title: Operation Focus
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: Egyptian airfields
markers.description: Operation Focus destroyed much of Egypt's air force on the ground in the opening hours.

markers.label: Sinai air bases
markers.description: Airfield attacks disabled Egyptian operations over Sinai.

markers.label: Jordan and Syria airfields
markers.description: After Jordanian and Syrian attacks, Israel struck their air bases too.

slides.title: Operation Focus
slides.body: Operation Focus was the opening airstrike by Israel at the start of the Six-Day War in 1967. It is sometimes referred to as the "Sinai Air Strike". At 07:45 on 5 June 1967, the Israeli Air Force (IAF) under Maj. Gen. Mordechai Hod launched a massive airstrike that destroyed the majority of the Egyptian Air Force on the ground. Following Syrian and Jordanian attacks in retaliation, the Israeli Air Force bombed air bases in those countries. By noon, the Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian Air Forces, totaling about 450 aircraft, were destroyed. It was also very successful in disabling 18 airfields in Egypt, hindering Egyptian air operations for the duration of the war, and remains one of the most successful air attack campaigns in military history. Operation Focus was Israel's decisive opening air strike, designed to destroy Arab air forces before they could threaten Israeli cities and troops.

stats.lbl: It gave Israel air superiority and shaped the entire war in its first hours.

slides.title: The Wider Impact
slides.body: It gave Israel air superiority and shaped the entire war in its first hours.

stats.lbl: It gave Israel air superiority and shaped the entire war in its first hours.

title: Battle of Ammunition Hill
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: Ammunition Hill
markers.description: One of the fiercest battles in Jerusalem, opening the way toward Mount Scopus and the Old City.

markers.label: Old City
markers.description: Israeli forces entered the Old City after the battle for East Jerusalem.

slides.title: Battle of Ammunition Hill
slides.body:
Ammunition Hill was a fortified Jordanian military post in the northern part of Jordanian-ruled East Jerusalem and the western slope of Mount Scopus. It was the site of one of the fiercest battles of the Six-Day War. Ammunition Hill is now a national memorial site. Ammunition Hill was one of the hardest fights in Jerusalem, where Israeli paratroopers battled for a fortified Jordanian position.

It opened the way to East Jerusalem and became a central symbol in Israeli memory.

stats.lbl: It opened the way to East Jerusalem and became a central symbol in Israeli memory.

title: Battle of Abu-Ageila
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: Abu-Ageila
markers.description: A key Egyptian defensive complex broken by Israeli combined-arms tactics.

markers.label: El Arish axis
markers.description: The breakthrough helped open the route across northern Sinai.

slides.title: Battle of Abu-Ageila
slides.body:
The Battle of Abu-Ageila was a military confrontation between the Israel Defense Forces and the Egyptian Army in the Six-Day War of June 1967. The decisive defeat of the Egyptians was critical to the eventual loss of the entire Sinai Peninsula to Israel. Leading Israeli forces was Major General Ariel Sharon, later a prominent politician and prime minister of Israel. Abu-Ageila was a key Egyptian defensive complex in Sinai, and Israeli victory there broke the backbone of the Egyptian front.

It allowed Israel to advance rapidly across Sinai and turned the southern campaign into a rout.

stats.lbl: It allowed Israel to advance rapidly across Sinai and turned the southern campaign into a rout.

title: Attack on an Iraqi Tupolev plane in Israel
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: Israeli airspace
markers.description: The Iraqi aircraft episode reflected Israeli fears that the war could expand beyond Egypt, Jordan, and Syria.

markers.label: Jordanian front
markers.description: Iraqi support was tied to the wider eastern-front danger facing Israel.

slides.title: Attack on an Iraqi Tupolev plane in Israel
slides.body:
The Iraqi aircraft incident reflected Israel's fear of wider Arab participation and the need to defend its airspace during a fast-moving war.

It showed how regional the conflict could become even beyond the main Egyptian, Jordanian, and Syrian fronts.

stats.lbl: It showed how regional the conflict could become even beyond the main Egyptian, Jordanian, and Syrian fronts.

title: Jordanian campaign
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: East Jerusalem
markers.description: The Jordanian front brought the war into Jerusalem and changed Israeli history dramatically.

markers.label: West Bank
markers.description: Jordanian-held territory was captured during the campaign.

markers.label: Jordan Valley
markers.description: Israeli forces pushed east as Jordanian resistance collapsed.

slides.title: Jordanian campaign
slides.body:
The Jordanian campaign of 1967 was part of the broader Six-Day War, in which Israel defeated Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Iraq. For Israel, it was the most significant part of the war, as it resulted in the capture of many Jewish monuments by the Israelis. The Jordanian front brought the war into Jerusalem and the West Bank after Jordan entered the fighting.

It changed Israel's map dramatically and placed Jerusalem at the center of the war's legacy.

stats.lbl: It changed Israel's map dramatically and placed Jerusalem at the center of the war's legacy.

title: USS Liberty incident
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: USS Liberty
markers.description: Israeli air and naval forces mistakenly attacked the American intelligence ship on 8 June 1967.

markers.label: Sinai coast
markers.description: The incident occurred while Israel was fighting fast-moving operations near Sinai.

slides.title: USS Liberty incident
slides.body:
The USS Liberty incident was an attack on a United States Navy technical research ship, USS Liberty, by Israeli Air Force jet fighter aircraft and Israeli Navy motor torpedo boats, on 8 June 1967, during the Six-Day War. The attack killed 34 crew members, wounded 171 crew members, and severely damaged the ship. Both the Israeli and United States governments conducted inquiries and issued reports that concluded the attack was a mistake due to Israeli confusion about the ship's identity. The USS Liberty incident was a tragic Israeli attack on an American intelligence ship during the fog of war.

It became a lasting diplomatic wound between Israel and the United States despite their broader strategic relationship.

stats.lbl: It became a lasting diplomatic wound between Israel and the United States despite their broader strategic relationship.

title: Battle of Tel Azaziat
sub: Israeli preemptive war and survival front

markers.label: Tel Azaziat
markers.description: A fortified Syrian post overlooking northern Israel.

markers.label: Golan Heights
markers.description: Capturing the heights removed a long-standing artillery threat to northern communities.

markers.label: Hula Valley
markers.description: Israeli communities below the heights had lived under Syrian fire.

slides.title: Battle of Tel Azaziat
slides.body:
Tel Azaziat was part of Israel's final push against Syrian positions overlooking northern communities.

It helped end the threat from the Golan Heights and reshaped Israel's northern security posture.

stats.lbl: It helped end the threat from the Golan Heights and reshaped Israel's northern security posture.

slides.title: War Summary: Six-Day War
slides.body:
Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights in six days. The speed was extraordinary because Israel began under blockade, reserve mobilization, and the fear of encirclement, then won air superiority in hours and used it to support rapid ground breakthroughs on three fronts.

The victory transformed Israel's strategic depth and morale, but it also created the central territorial and political disputes that shaped the next decades: control of the territories, Jerusalem, settlements, refugees, and the search for peace with neighboring states.

stats.lbl: Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights. The dramatic territorial changes reshaped every later stage of the conflict.
